body:
With `ensure_ascii`, the `json_view` dump wrote every string through the escaping path, which decodes UTF-8 byte by byte. It did so even for strings of the source that are plain ASCII. Without `ensure_ascii`, those strings are already copied verbatim.

A string of the source without escape sequences has no quote, backslash or control character. `ensure_ascii` therefore leaves it unchanged exactly when no byte is `0x7F` or above. The dump now checks that eight bytes at a time (`is_ascii_without_delete()`: `(v | (v + 0x01…01)) & 0x80…80`, which flags bytes ≥ 0x80 and DEL) and copies such strings and keys the same way as without `ensure_ascii`. The compact walk (`dump_compact`), which used to serve only the dump without `ensure_ascii`, now serves `ensure_ascii` too. It does so through a separate out-of-line instantiation, so the walk without `ensure_ascii` keeps its speed.

With GCC, adding the check as one combined condition, `!enabled(Ascii) || …`, changed the block layout of the walk without `ensure_ascii`, even though the condition is folded away there. That made it 4–6% slower in cycle counts. One `copied()` overload per `std::integral_constant` keeps its machine code identical to `develop`.

## Alternative considered

The parser could record "all ASCII" in a free node flag, since the scanner branches on bytes ≥ 0x80 anyway. The dump would then not need to check anything. That made compact `ensure_ascii` output about twice as fast again: B/A 0.29–0.58 instead of 0.44–0.67. But it also needed a cached `memchr` for DEL per document and image changes, and it made `json_document::parse` of string-heavy input 1–2% slower with GCC (about 1.4 instructions per string). Parsing matters to every user, and `ensure_ascii` only to some, so this PR leaves the parser alone.

## Performance

`json_document::root().dump()` of the parsed (minified) file, against `develop`. B/A is the ratio of medians from interleaved A/B runs, 10–12 rounds each; below 1 is faster.

With `ensure_ascii`, compact / indent 4:

| | twitter | citm_catalog | jeopardy | canada (floats) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple M1, Apple Clang | 0.668 / 0.909 | 0.435 / 0.914 | 0.558 / 0.857 | 0.943 / 1.003 |
| Apple M1, GCC 16 | 0.653 / 0.914 | 0.485 / 0.936 | 0.574 / 0.869 | 0.912 / 1.001 |
| x86-64 (Haswell VPS), Clang 18 | 0.713 / 0.840 | 0.500 / 0.849 | 0.783 / 0.821 | 0.979 / 1.006 |
| x86-64 (Haswell VPS), GCC 13 | 0.629 / 0.818 | 0.416 / 0.805 | 0.761 / 0.823 | 0.977 / 1.013 |

Without `ensure_ascii` (compact and indent 4, all four files):

- On the M1, every row is between 0.986 and 1.007.
- On the VPS, every row is between 0.982 and 1.019. That machine had other load, with spreads of 5–17%.
- Cycle counts on the M1 are within ±0.5%.

Parsing is not touched.

## Tests

Two new sections in `unit-json_view_dump.cpp`:

- **Mixed documents.** A document with plain, non-ASCII, escaped and long strings, as values and as keys, is compared with `ordered_json::dump()` for compact, indented and subtree dumps. The document is tested once with a DEL and once without, and also with strings that edits changed to and from ASCII.
- **Every position.** DEL, `0x7E` and two 2-byte characters are placed at every position of strings of 1–20 bytes, as values and as keys, which covers the 8-byte steps and the tail loop. As a check that the test can fail, treating DEL as ASCII makes 423 assertions fail.

Also run locally:

- all `unit-json_view*` tests with ASan and UBSan;
- a differential test of 400,000 random documents (ASCII, DEL, escapes, 2/3/4-byte characters, surrogate escapes) against `ordered_json::dump(-1/2, ' ', true)`, with 0 mismatches;
- GCC 16 and Clang 22 with the CI warning flags;
- clang-tidy 22 on `unit-json_view_dump.cpp`.

## Public API

No breaking changes. The output of `dump()` is unchanged.

The one corner case: a damaged image loaded with `image_check::bounds` can contain control characters in source strings. With `ensure_ascii`, these are now copied unchanged, as the dump without `ensure_ascii` already does for such images.

---

This pull request was written by Claude Code.

comments.body:
>The parser could record "all ASCII" in a free node flag, since the scanner branches on bytes ≥ 0x80 anyway. The dump would then not need to check anything. That made compact ensure_ascii output about twice as fast again: B/A 0.29–0.58 instead of 0.44–0.67. But it also needed a cached memchr for DEL per document and image changes, and it made json_document::parse of string-heavy input 1–2% slower with GCC (about 1.4 instructions per string).

Can you expand more on this "needed a cached memchr for DEL per document and image changes"?

Sure. The scanner only branches on bytes ≥ 0x80, so a node flag set from there means "no byte ≥ 0x80". But `ensure_ascii` also escapes DEL (0x7F), so a string with that flag still can't be copied as is if it contains a DEL. Checking for 0x7F in the scanner would add work to every parse, which is what I wanted to avoid. So the prototype searched the whole source once with `memchr(src, 0x7F, size)` on the first `ensure_ascii` dump, and cached the answer in `document_data`. It's an atomic because two threads can dump the same `const` document at once. The flag only lets the dump copy a string when the source has no DEL at all. The SWAR check in this PR has no such problem, because `v + 0x01…` turns 0x7F into 0x80 and so catches DEL too.

"Image changes" means the saved image (`save_image()` / `load()`). The flag takes a new node bit. `load()` validates node flags and would reject that bit, and the same document should save to the same bytes whether or not it has the flag. So `save_image()` had to clear the bit on every string node, which is one more per-node case in the save loop. The alternative was a format change so that `load()` accepts the bit.

Neither part is large, but together with the 1–2% slower GCC parse, that was more than I wanted to add to the parser for an option only some users need.

*(Written by Claude Code)*

Okay, so there is nothing in `parse` that already detects `DEL` that can be used to record that during parse, and the same for edits and `load()`?  

Since `load/save` was just merged today, is "a format change" really an issue?

You're right on both counts: nothing on those paths looks at 0x7F, and since json_view hasn't been released, a format change costs nothing. That argument was weak.

So I prototyped it without that constraint: the scanner stops at DEL as well (`(int8)(b + 1) < 0x21` in the vector loop), the parser sets an "all ASCII" node flag, `load()` accepts it, and the dump uses the flag instead of the SWAR check. No `memchr`, no atomic. Results against current develop, as instruction counts:

- compact `ensure_ascii` dump: 0.68–0.88× (M1), 0.74–0.90× (x86)
- `json_document::parse`: +1–8% (M1), +5–13% (x86, GCC 13 and Clang 18), most on string-heavy files (jeopardy)

On x86, most of the cost is recording the flag at all, not the DEL check: a variant that flags only bytes ≥ 0x80 costs the same. My earlier 1–2% estimate predates the SIMD string scanner (#5853). Against it, the flag is relatively much more expensive. So the format wasn't the real obstacle, but the parse cost is, and I'd keep #5879 as is.

*(Written by Claude Code)*

Just trying to understand the cost.  Was the cost because it was adding a new test that wasn't there before? Or was it adjusting an existing test to cover one more byte, but that somehow made it a lot more expensive?

Neither, really. Most of it is how the compilers lay out the loop, not the instructions the change adds. Per string or key, measured on jeopardy (3.04M of them):

- **Flag only for bytes ≥ 0x80:** no new test. The scanner already branches to the UTF-8 path on those bytes, and the flag is a store in that branch plus passing the result to `push_node()`, which used to get a constant 0. That's +1.5 instructions on the M1 (Clang) but +11–13 on x86 (GCC 13, Clang 18). That's far more than a store and a select, so the compilers generate different code around the parse loop. I suspect register pressure, as we saw in #5853, but I haven't compared the x86 assembly.
- **Including DEL** widens existing tests instead of adding new ones: one more add per 16 bytes in the vector compare (about +2 instructions per string on the M1), and the stop test `*p < 0x80` becomes `*p < 0x7F`, with DEL handled in the non-ASCII branch (about +4 more). On x86 it adds almost nothing on top of the flag.

So the expensive part on x86 is getting a per-string result out of the inlined scanner at all, not the extra byte.

*(Written by Claude Code)*
Thanks, that's all very interesting.  Optimizers can definitely be black boxes.

review_comments.body:
Yes, it surprised me too. When both walks are in one function, GCC lays out the blocks differently and stops inlining the small helpers in the hot loop, so the walk without `ensure_ascii` gets slower even though that branch is never taken. Keeping the `ensure_ascii` walk in its own function leaves the plain walk's code as it was.

*(Written by Claude Code)*

title: Copy ASCII strings in the json_view dump with ensure_ascii
